notes:
I read Enduring Word (Guzik), Precept Austin, and the Bible Hub and StudyLight pages that collect the older commentaries (Calvin, Matthew Henry, Gill, Barnes, Pulpit, Ellicott, Clarke, JFB, Poole, Constable, Utley). I couldn't reach any Catholic or Orthodox page (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, or any Lutheran, Pentecostal or Wesleyan site, so those views are left out. The verses are grouped the way the commentators group them.

**vv. 1–3: Leaders who eat their people**
- **The leaders are singled out.** Guzik says Micah now addresses the leaders because they had both a special responsibility and accountability before God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-3/
- **"Should you not know justice?"** Waltke (quoted by Precept Austin) says "know" means more than knowing the law in your head. It means personally knowing it, so that out of sympathy for the victim you punish the wrongdoer and restore the outcast. https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_3_commentary
- **Calvin on rulers.** Without the Spirit of God, the acutest men are wholly unfit to rule. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/3-1.html
- **Who is addressed.** Clarke sees the shepherd-and-flock picture continuing from ch. 2: rulers who should guard the sheep tear them like wolves. Coffman, citing Leslie Allen, says the names "Jacob" and "Israel" here mean Judah, the southern kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/3-1.html
- **The cannibal picture.** Waltke (via Guzik) explains it: the poor were being ground into early graves, so Micah pictures the officials who caused this as cannibals. Guzik's lesson is that the people never exist for the sake of the leaders, but leaders are there for the sake of the people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-3/
- **Not literal.** Precept Austin calls the image clearly figurative, a common way of describing oppression (Ps 14:4). It is meant to wake up the leaders' consciences. https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_3_commentary
- **Henry on breaking the bones.** They break the bones to get at the marrow. This shows rulers who were greedy and self-indulgent, and cruel to those under them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/3-1.html
- **Calvin on power.** Because rulers hold power, they ought to be a law to themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/micah-3.html

**v. 4: God will not answer**
- **The punishment fits the crime.** Henry: they shall have judgment without mercy that have shown no mercy. God will not hear them, just as they would not hear the poor. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/3-1.html
- **Hiding his face.** Guzik says this is the reverse of the priestly blessing in Num 6:25, where God's face shines on his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-3/
- **Calvin** calls it the greatest evil that could happen to us: God rejects those who reject Him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_3_commentary
- **When is "then"?** Precept Austin suggests the Assyrian conquest of the north (722 BC) and the Babylonian conquest of Judah (586 BC). https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_3_commentary

**v. 5: Prophets for hire**
- **Meaning.** The prophets promise peace to whoever feeds them and threaten those who don't (Clarke; JFB). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/3-5.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Mic/Mic_003.cfm
- **Utley.** They prophesy for hire, not for God. They tell rich clients what they want to hear. https://bible.org/seriespage/micah-3
- **Gill's other readings.** "Bite with their teeth" could also mean the prophets hold back the disasters they can see coming, or snarl at the true prophets. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/micah/3-5.html

**vv. 6–7: Darkness and silence**
- **The punishment matches the sin.** Allen says those who abused their gifts lose them. Precept Austin points out the irony: night, when they claimed to get visions, is exactly when their visions stop. https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_3_commentary
- **"Divination."** Precept Austin says Micah is not approving divination, which Dt 18:10 forbids. He is saying even their occult methods will fail. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61009/
- **Covering their mouths.** Calvin (via JFB) reads this as shame: they will not dare open their mouths or call themselves prophets. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/micah-3.html

**v. 8: Micah's power from the Spirit**
- **The three gifts.** Barnes: "power" expresses the divine might lodged in him; "judgment," the substance of what he had to deliver; "might or courage," the strength to deliver it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/3-8.htm
- **No boasting.** The Pulpit Commentary says Micah gives the credit to the Spirit, not himself. Henry says those who act honestly can act boldly. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/micah-3.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_003.cfm
- **Waltke:** “The sign of being filled with the Spirit is speaking of justice”. https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_3_commentary

**Where the traditions differ (v. 8): does this verse apply to preachers and prophets today?**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Anyone who wants to be a teacher in the church must be endued with the Spirit of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/micah-3.html
- **JFB:** Ministers do not have the prophet's miraculous inspiration, but every minister taught by the Spirit can still say these words. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/micah-3.html
- **Guzik (Enduring Word, listed among your Pentecostal/charismatic sites):** Prophets under the new covenant have a somewhat different calling. New Testament prophecy aims at edification, exhortation and comfort (1 Cor 14:3). It may still expose sin, but that isn't its central purpose. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-3/

**vv. 9–10: Building Zion with blood**
- **Mays (via Precept Austin):** “It was urban renewal with a vengeance, a new Jerusalem that cost the lives of men.” https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_3_commentary
- **Henry:** They perverted equity by doing obvious wrongs while claiming to do right. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_003.cfm

**v. 11: Bribes, and false confidence**
- **Priests teaching for a price.** Patterson (via Precept Austin) says this means money paid for priestly rulings on the Law of Moses. https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_commentaries
- **Henry on "leaning on the LORD."** Faith builds on the Lord as its foundation. Presumption only *leans upon the Lord* as a prop, while the world is the real foundation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_003.cfm
- **Bible Hub notes:** They had faith without love, divorced religion from morality. https://biblehub.com/micah/3-11.htm
- **Precept Austin:** God's promise to live among them was conditional on obedience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_3_commentary

**v. 12: Zion plowed like a field**
- **Quoted a century later.** Jeremiah 26:18 quotes this verse. Hezekiah took it to heart and repented, so the judgment did not come in his day (Bible Hub; Henry). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/3-12.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/3-12.html
- **A unique quotation.** The Cambridge notes on Jeremiah call it the only place in the prophets where another prophet is quoted by name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-18.htm
- **Barnes:** They thought to be its builders; they were its destroyers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/3-12.html
- **Utley:** This is the first prophecy of Jerusalem's fall. People were shocked because they believed God had promised Jerusalem and the temple would never fall. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/micah-3.html

**Where the commentators differ (v. 12): was it fulfilled?** This is a split between commentators, not clearly between denominations.
- **Delayed by repentance, then fulfilled in stages.** Gill: put off when the people repented, partly fulfilled by the Babylonians, more fully by the Romans. Barnes adds Jewish accounts of the temple site being plowed under the Romans and travellers who saw Zion farmed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/3-12.html
- **Fulfilled in 586 BC.** Bible Hub's study notes say so. https://biblehub.com/micah/3-12.htm
- **Never completely fulfilled.** The Pulpit Commentary says the threat was conditional, like all such judgments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/3-12.htm
- **Repentance meant it was not carried out.** A note on Jeremiah 26:18 says the elders' point was that the threat did its work and so was not carried out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-18.htm

**Popular modern teaching (vv. 5, 11)**
- **Prosperity gospel.** Precept Austin's editor compares the paid "peace" prophets to the modern day "prosperity gospel!" and to "televangelists." https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61009/
- **Kingcomments** says these prophets promise prosperity in proportion to the money they receive. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/micah/3.htm

These are the critics' descriptions; I found no pages defending prosperity teaching on this passage.
